author: Delaney Eyermann
title: Missouri resident diagnosed with rare 'brain-eating' infection: DHSS - NewsBreak
text: KANSAS CITY, Mo. (WDAF) — A Missouri resident has been diagnosed with a laboratory-confirmed infection of Naegleria fowleri, the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services (DHSS) announced Wednesday. Naegleria fowleri is a microscopic single-celled, free-living ameba that can cause a rare, deadly infection of the brain called primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), also known as a “brain-eating” infection. DHSS said typically, fewer than 10 people a year in the United States get PAM. The Missouri patient is currently being treated for PAM in an intensive care unit of a hospital. Currently, DHSS said there are no additional suspected cases of PAM being investigated in Missouri. The ameba is common and naturally present in warm freshwater, such as lakes, rivers and ponds; however, PAM is extremely rare. Between 1962 and 2024, there were 167 reported cases in the United States. The source of the patient’s exposure is currently being investigated by public health officials. Although not confirmed, preliminary information implies the patient may have been water skiing at the Lake of the Ozarks days prior to becoming ill. Recreational water users should assume that Naegleria fowleri is present in warm freshwater across the United States. Although rare in occurrence, people become infected by Naegleria fowleri when water containing the ameba enters the body through the nose from freshwater sources. The Naegleria fowleri ameba then travels up the nose to the brain, where it damages the brain tissue. While it can be deadly, Dr. Dana Hawkinson at The University of Kansas Health System isn’t sounding alarm bells about the infection. “We do have to understand that, especially in the summertime when people are out in those small freshwater bodies, whether it’s a pond or a lake, there is that small risk,” he said. “Certainly, we know the risk of this infection is low is much lower than compared to a lot of things. But there is a risk there.” Dr. Hawkinson is the medical director of infection prevention and control for the health system and says that diagnosing PAM is difficult. “Some of the presentation, why it makes it so difficult, is because it is just generalized symptoms,” he said. “You may feel bad, you may feel rundown, and then, of course, it can progress to that central nervous system infection.” DHSS says that if people experience severe headaches, fever, nausea, vomiting or an altered mental status after swimming in warm bodies of water, they should contact their health provider. Hawkinson said treatment is equally as challenging. “Because it is so rare, we don’t have a lot of information on it. We know that the treatment consists of antibacterial medication, antifungal medication, and antiparasitic medication, all in combination. But even those combinations don’t have a very good or high rate of cure for this as well.” He says there are precautions that people can take to protect themselves from infection. “If you do go underwater again, try not to inhale it,” Hawkinson said. “You know, some people will say either plug up your nose or blow outward because we don’t want it going in through your nasal passages. That’s where it is able to come into contact with that small barrier between your brain, and that’s how it gets into the central nervous system.” DHSS also recommends avoiding stirring up sediment in warm freshwater areas, where the amoebas are more likely to live. This infection cannot be spread from one person to another, and it cannot be contracted by swallowing contaminated water. People can take actions to reduce the risk of infection by limiting the amount of water going up the nose.
